summary: This memo presents an architecture for inter-domain policy routing, in which routes between networks can be chosen according to the policies of each network. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This paper is the blueprint for a system that picks routes between networks according to each network's rules. It is historic.

questions: what is idpr inter-domain policy routing
subtitle: Let networks choose routes according to their own policies instead of just following the shortest path.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, different administrative domains needed to apply their own policies to routing—some domains might require higher quality of service, others might restrict access, and others might charge for transit. Traditional routing protocols ignore these policies.
tldr.mechanism: IDPR defines an architecture where networks can exchange policy information via link state messages, and source domains compute routes that satisfy their own policies while respecting the restrictions of transit domains. Messages are forwarded according to source-specified paths that cannot be rerouted at intermediate hops.
tldr.outcome: The architecture supports routing in a large heterogeneous Internet with tens of thousands of autonomous domains, each applying their own service restrictions and requirements. This RFC is Historic.

today: RFC 1478 is a Historic protocol. IDPR proposed a comprehensive architecture but was overtaken by simpler approaches like BGP policy extensions, which achieved market adoption. The RFC remains a foundational reference for understanding policy routing concepts.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Inter-Domain Policy Routing (IDPR) is an architecture for routing between administrative domains that respects each domain's policies. An administrative domain is any collection of networks governed by a single authority that chooses how traffic can flow through it.

Traditional routing protocols find the shortest path and assume all network administrators have the same goals. But in a large Internet with thousands of independent domains, each domain has its own policies: some domains offer premium quality of service for a fee, others restrict access to certain customers, and all have resource limits.

IDPR lets each domain set transit policies (what services it offers and who can use them) and source policies (what services a domain's own traffic requires and which domains to avoid). Path selection happens at the source and respects all these constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a message across many networks, each network has its own rules about what kinds of messages it will carry and what it charges. This describes a system where the sender picks a path that obeys all those rules from the start.

sections.title: Routing Design Choices
sections.content:
IDPR evaluates two main approaches to policy routing and selects specific strategies for each.

For route generation (computing the path), IDPR chooses link state over distance vector. With link state, each domain advertises its transit policies and connectivity to neighboring domains. The source domain collects this information and computes its own routes, keeping its source policies private. Distance vector would force source domains to share their policies with every intermediate domain, increasing overhead and exposing private preferences.

For message forwarding (sending traffic), IDPR chooses source-specified forwarding over hop-by-hop. With hop-by-hop, each router independently picks the next hop, which works only if all routers share consistent routing information—difficult when domains keep policies private. With source-specified forwarding, the source domain specifies the entire path or uses path identifiers, guaranteeing that each message follows the intended route regardless of what other domains know.

This combination ensures source policies are respected and prevents routing loops even when different domains have incomplete information.
sections.plainLanguage: The system uses two key ideas: domains tell each other what they offer and how they connect, and the sender picks the whole path at the start so it cannot be rerouted along the way.

sections.title: The IDPR Architecture
sections.content:
IDPR defines three main types of entities. Policy gateways are physical routers at the boundary between domains. Multiple policy gateways can form a virtual gateway, the only inter-domain connection point recognized by IDPR, providing redundancy and load sharing.

Path agents act on behalf of hosts or domains to select routes and set up paths. They query route servers for suitable policy routes given the source and destination domains and requested services.

IDPR servers manage databases: route servers maintain routing information and generate policy routes on request; mapping servers resolve Internet addresses to domain identities; configuration servers distribute source and transit policies and IDPR entity information within a domain.

The architecture supports a domain not running IDPR by using an IDPR proxy: a neighboring domain's path agents select routes on behalf of the non-IDPR domain's hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers at the edges between domains are the gateways; each domain has special agents that pick paths for their traffic; and separate servers keep track of policies, connectivity, and routes.

sections.title: Route Generation
sections.content:
Route generation in IDPR is computationally complex because it must satisfy requested service constraints (maximum delay, minimum bandwidth) and optimize for requested preferences (minimum delay, minimum cost) while respecting all transit domains' access restrictions.

Route servers apply several strategies to manage complexity: they generate routes only from their own domain as the source, precompute routes they anticipate will be requested, and cache results. When handling multiple constraints and preferences, servers first satisfy all requested limits, then optimize according to specified preferences in order of importance.

Importantly, domain administrators are free to implement their own route generation algorithms, ranging from simple to sophisticated. The architecture does not mandate a single procedure; it only specifies that routes must respect the constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding a route that satisfies all the rules from all the networks is hard work, so each network does its own route-finding for traffic starting in its domain, and saves the answers so it does not have to recompute them.

sections.title: Supporting Thousands of Domains
sections.content:
IDPR employs several mechanisms to scale to a very large Internet.

Domain-level routing means IDPR routing databases need only track domain-to-domain connectivity and transit policies, not individual networks or links within each domain. This dramatically reduces the size of routing tables.

Super domains allow groups of adjacent domains with similar transit policies to be managed as one, further reducing routing information. Domain communities let administrators limit the distribution of their routing information to selected neighbors, reducing costs of dissemination and storage.

IDPR servers organize their databases hierarchically, with local servers tracking one domain, global servers tracking all domains, and intermediate levels in between. This relieves most servers from maintaining information about the entire Internet.

Path repair lets policy gateways quickly recover from link failures by finding alternate routes locally, and partition detection lets IDPR operate even when a domain is split by a connectivity failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of tracking every tiny network, IDPR tracks just which domains connect to which and groups similar domains together. Servers only keep information they actually need, and when something breaks, gateways can find quick detours.

sections.title: Security and Reliability
sections.content:
IDPR includes mechanisms to ensure correct control information propagates and is not corrupted or forged.

All IDPR control messages require acknowledgements, and senders retransmit unacknowledged messages up to a maximum number of times. Recipients verify message integrity (version, length, checksum) and timestamp validity before accepting messages. The architecture recommends that sources digitally sign IDPR control messages so recipients can authenticate the sender.

Every IDPR control message must carry a timestamp. IDPR entities check that timestamps are current and use relative differences between timestamps to select the most recent routing information. Clock synchronization is required to the granularity of minutes, achievable through manual adjustment.

These measures reduce the risk of routing information corruption and denial-of-service attacks while maintaining the decentralized nature of the architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages need a receipt stamp saying where they came from and when, and receivers check that nothing was scrambled. This stops bad actors from fooling the system into using wrong routes.
